```{python}
import polars as pl 
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
import polars.selectors as cs
# add the additional libraries you need to import for ML here

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
```

<!-- The first 10 rows are not part of the datset we need.

The columns headers are split across two rows. We need to clean and simplify the column headers-->

```{python}
# Read in and tidy up the first row
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))
# Note the non-ascii character in the column "Do you consider yourself to be a fan of the Expanded Universe". (column AF if you open it in Excel). 

# BTW: Detecting what it is and where can be difficult

# Lossy means that invalid utf8 values are replaced with � characters. When using other encodings than utf8 or utf8-lossy, the input is first decoded in memory with python. Defaults to utf8...ignore_errors = True does not replace the non-utf8 character with a blank space like you would hope

a[2] = "seen_any" #simply overwrite the value at index 2

# Rather than changing each column header manually,
# here we use regex to apply changes more efficiently
a = (
  a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
   .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
   .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
   .fill_null(strategy = "forward")

   .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "") #this gets rid of the question marks in a diamond characters 
   .str.strip_chars()
   .str.to_lowercase()
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")

)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"
```

<!-- Combine series q and a into one series to be used as column names-->

```{python}
b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))

b = (
  b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
   .str.replace("Response", "")
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .fill_null("")
   .str.strip_chars()
)

```

```{python}
#Now combine the two series, each of which contains part of the desired column header
new_names = (a + b).to_list()

# Read in the data, skipping over the column header rows
# and use 'new_names' as the column headers
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns = new_names )
```

## Methods

_This first chunk of code gleans first and last names from various email types. This is for user convenience rather than a machine learning algorithm._

```{python}
regexmap = [r'(?i)([A-Z]+)',r'[\._0-9](?i)([A-Z]+)',r'@(?i)([A-Z]+)']
adf = (
  df.with_columns(
    (pl.col("email").str.extract(regexmap[2]).str.to_lowercase()).alias("domain")
  )
  .with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("domain")=="gmail")
    .then(pl.col("email").str.extract(regexmap[0]))
    .otherwise(pl.col("email").str.extract(regexmap[1]))
    .alias("first"),

    pl.when(pl.col("domain") == "gmail")
    .then(pl.col("email").str.extract(regexmap[1]))
    .otherwise(pl.col("email").str.extract(regexmap[0]))
    .alias("last")
  )
).select("email","first","last","domain")
bdf = (
  adf.group_by("domain")
  .agg(pl.len().alias("count"))
  .sort(by=["count"],descending=True)
)
adf.head().show()
bdf.head().show()
```

_This chunk of code is a compilation of numerical replacements for non-numeric yet easily translatable items such as a range of favorability or level of education. These replacements will be beneficial to the machine as their value directly correlates with the string option. The remaining string options will be cared for in the next code block._
```{python}
#i am so sorry for the wall below this
yesnomap = {None:0,"No":0,"Yes":1}
favorabilitymap = {None:0,"Unfamiliar (N/A)":0,"Very unfavorably":1,"Somewhat unfavorably":2,"Neither favorably nor unfavorably (neutral)":3,"Somewhat favorably":4,"Very favorably":5}
#hanshotfirst = {None:0,"I don't understand this question":0,"Greedo":1,"Han":2}
# gendermap = {"Male":0,"Female":1}
edumap = {None:0,"Less than high school degree":1,"High school degree":2,"Some college or Associate degree":3,"Bachelor degree":4,"Graduate degree":5}
#locmap = {None:0,"East South Central":1,"New England":2,"Mountain":3,"West North Central":4,"West South Central":5,"Middle Atlantic":6,"South Atlantic":7,"Pacific":8,"East North Central":9}
cdf = (
  df.filter(pl.any_horizontal(cs.starts_with("seen_Episode_").is_not_null()))
  .drop_nulls(subset=["age"]+[f"rank_Episode_{r}" for r in ["I","II","III","IV","V","VI"]])
  .with_columns(
    pl.col("star_wars_fan","know_expanded_universe","expanded_universe_fan","star_trek_fan").replace(yesnomap).cast(pl.Int8),
    cs.starts_with("seen_Episode").is_not_null().cast(pl.Int8),
    cs.starts_with("rank_Episode").cast(pl.Int8),
    pl.col("fav_Han_Solo","fav_Luke_Skywalker","fav_Princess_Leia_Organa","fav_Anakin_Skywalker","fav_Obi_Wan_Kenobi","fav_Emperor_Palpatine","fav_Darth_Vader","fav_Lando_Calrissian","fav_Boba_Fett","fav_C-3P0","fav_R2_D2","fav_Jar_Jar_Binks","fav_Padme_Amidala","fav_Yoda").replace(favorabilitymap).cast(pl.Int8),
    #pl.col("who_shot_first").replace(hanshotfirst).cast(pl.Int8),
    # pl.col("gender").replace(gendermap).cast(pl.Int8),
    pl.col("age").str.extract_all(r"\d+").cast(pl.List(pl.Float64)).list.mean().cast(pl.Float16),
    pl.col("household_income").fill_null(0).str.replace_all(",","").str.extract_all(r"\d+").cast(pl.List(pl.Float64)).list.mean().round().cast(pl.Int32),
    pl.col("education").replace(edumap).cast(pl.Int8),
    #pl.col("location").replace(locmap).cast(pl.Int8)
  )
  
  .drop("seen_any")
)
df.show()
cdf.show()
```

_The remaining string values do not have any spectrum numerically, so must be cared for using OneHotEncoding. It creates new columns for each string value of the original dataframe, assigning 1 if it was the value listed in the column, 0 if otherwise. This will be more beneficial to the machine learning model as it indicates no correlation or equal correlation between all previous string values._
```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

performOn = ["who_shot_first","gender","location"]
ohe = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown='ignore')
new = pl.from_numpy(
  ohe.fit_transform(cdf[performOn]),
  schema=ohe.get_feature_names_out(performOn).tolist()
).cast(pl.Int8)
ddf = (
  cdf.hstack(new)
  .with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("household_income")>5e4)
    .then(1)
    .otherwise(0)
    .alias("makes_over_50k")
    .cast(pl.Int8)
  )
  .drop("respondentid","email","who_shot_first","gender","household_income","location")
)
ddf.show()
```

_This chunk of code trains four different models on the data above. It compares the makes\_over\_50k column with all other columns to create the best model of its type. See each model's accuracy in the __Results__ section._
```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
  ddf.select(pl.exclude("makes_over_50k")),
  ddf["makes_over_50k"],
  test_size=0.2,
  random_state=0
)

forestModel = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100,max_depth=5,random_state=0)
forestModel.fit(X_train, y_train)
forestPredict = forestModel.predict(X_test)

xgbModel = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=100,learning_rate=0.05,max_depth=5,random_state=0)
xgbModel.fit(X_train, y_train)
xgbPredict = xgbModel.predict(X_test)

NBModel = GaussianNB()
NBModel.fit(X_train, y_train)
NBPredict = NBModel.predict(X_test)

gradientBoostModel = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100,learning_rate=0.05,max_depth=5,random_state=0)
gradientBoostModel.fit(X_train, y_train)
gradientBoostPredict = gradientBoostModel.predict(X_test)
```

## Results

_A small amount of tinkering was done on the machile learning models, however non-extensive. It was found that most models averaged around 55% accurate. The top performing model is seen to be the Random Forest model. It achieved a 60% accuracy at a lower test size and higher tree depth. Such a low accuracy score can indicate two possibilities. One possibility is that someone's opinion on Star Wars may not be a good indicator for household income. Another possibility is that there was insufficient data collected, such as too little size datasets or irrelevant questions being asked. However, since many questions were asked in the survey, the first possibility is more likely._

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
modelResults = pl.DataFrame({
  "Models": ["Random Forest","XGBoost","Naive Bayes","Gradient Boosting"],
  "Accuracy":[accuracy_score(y_test,forestPredict),accuracy_score(y_test,xgbPredict),accuracy_score(y_test,NBPredict),accuracy_score(y_test,gradientBoostPredict)]
}).sort(by=["Accuracy"],descending=True).show()
```
